texts.facts: The facts in brief are that Sh.Bal Mukund, Food Safety Officer("FSO" in short) purchased the item "Tomato Ketchup" from FBOcumManager Sh.Raj Mal Thakur S/o Late Sh.Het Ram, M/s Fujiya Restaurant, 12/48, Malcha Marge Market, New Delhi110021 on 04.01.2018 as per due procedure for analysis under the provisions of FSS Act & Regulation 2011. The Food Analyst vide his report no.FSS/21/2018 dated 18.01.2018 opined that the sample is misbranded because there is violation of Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011 ["FSS (P&L) Regulations" in short]. The Food Analyst also reported about label class title with specific name or recognised international number system for preservatives was not declared on the label. The appellant no.1 is FBO cum Assistant Manager of M/s Fujiya Restaurant(appellant no.3 FBO firm), appellant no.2 is partner of appellant no.3, appellant no.4 is proprietor to supplier firm to appellant no.3, appellant no.5 is nominee of appellant no.6(manufacturing company/supplier to appellant no.4). The FSO filed a complaint before the Ld.ADM, New Delhi under 3.1.1(3) of The Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011("FSS Rules" in short) against the appellants for adjudication of the offence u/S 23(1), 26(1), 26(2)(ii), 27(1) and 27(2)(c) r/w Section 3(1) (zf) (C ) (i) of FSS Act alongwith violation of Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulations which is punishable u/S 52 of FSS Act. In Accordance with the rules, the FBO was served the notice under Rule 3.1.1.(3) of FSS Rules alongwith copy of the report of Food Analyst, affording him an opportunity of being heard. Ld . ADM
texts.arguments: 3. Aggrieved by the impugned order, the appellants have filed the present appeal challenging the impugned order on the grounds that the Ld.ADM did not appreciate the law that the offence of misbranding under Regulation No.2.2.2.5(i) of FSS (P&L) Regulations is made out only when food additive is added to food article and its INS number is not declared on the label. In this case, in the Tomato Ketchup class II preservative was neither added by manufacturer nor it was found in the sample by the Food Analyst. Therefore, it is not the case that food additive was added in the sample and INS number was not mentioned on the label. Merely because superfluous wrongful declaration of food additive, which is class II preservative which was not even added to Tomato Ketchup and was not found in sample by Food Analyst, there was no point of giving any INS number. It has been submitted that in this case, Acetic acid(INS260) which not only acts as acidifying agent but also as class I preservative was used to preserve the Tomato Ketchup by the manufacturer instead of class II preservative, therefore, writing of INS number of class II preservative was not required to be printed as per law and hence, not written/printed. It has been submitted that the directions of FSSAI for minor labeling offences was not considered which u/S 16(5) of FSS Act are binding upon the Commissioners of Food Safety and other stakeholders. It has been submitted that the appellants no.1 to 4 were entitled to defense of due diligence u/S 80 of FSS Act but the same has not been granted. It has been further submitted that the Delhi Food Laboratory in which this sample Shri Rajmal Thakur S/O Late Shri Het Ram vs Food Safety Officer on 19 August, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45818632/ 2 commodity was analysed and issued analytical report in this case, was not legally competent lab to analyze the samples of food under FSS Act as per Section 43 of FSS Act as the same is neither NABL Accredited nor notified in Official Gazettee as per provisions of Section 3 (1)(p) FSS Act. Ld. ADM has also not adjudicated the validity of lab as per law and application for summoning of Food Analyst for cross examination was also ignored which is prejudicial to appellants. Moreover, report of Food Analyst is also not admissible as per provisions of FSS Act unless proved by the Food Analyst as the same is not conclusive as per Evidence Act unlike PFA Act 1954 which now stands repealed. Therefore, it should not have been read in evidence against the appellants for imposing any penalty. 4. Ld.Counsel for the appellants has submitted that since the Class II preservative which is a Food additive not found present in the sample by the Food Analyst, therefore, non writing of class title with international numbering system, looses its significance and therefore, there is no case of misbranding. It was also stated that when FSO took the sample, it was in sealed state and not tempered one in any manner and was in the state as were manufactured and supplied by appellants no.5 &6 to appellants no.1 to 4 with valid invoices and therefore, there is complete compliance of defense of due diligence as per Section 80(B) (2) (a) (i) and (ii) d (i) and (e) and therefore, appellants no.1 to 4 are entitled to be given benefit in this regard. The appellants also took the plea that the Food Lab at Delhi where the sample was analysed was neither NABL accredited nor the same was notified as per Section 43 FSS Act. 5. Per contra, Ld.Chief PP has submitted that due opportunity was given to the appellants to file an appeal against the report of Food Analyst. However, this opportunity was not availed and therefore, the report of Food Analyst was duly accepted. It has been submitted that the Ld.ADM has duly appreciated the facts and rightly punished the appellants. 6. Thus, the case of the appellants can be summed up by saying that since there was no class II preservative, therefore, nonmentioning of INS number on the label would not bring the case within the ambit of misbranding. The second contention is that the defence of due diligence as provided u/S 80 FSS Act should have been given to the appellants no.1 to 4. The case of the department/respondent can be summed up by saying that the provision of FSS Act are required to be adhered strictly and any deviation from the requirements of this Act, has to be adjudicated in accordance with law. It has further been submitted that the purpose of Act is primarily to defend the rights of the consumer and therefore, it needs strict interpretation. 8. In State of Kerala Vs. Parameswaram Pillai Vasudevan Nair, 1975 Cri LJ 97, it was interalia held as under: "14.The Act is a piece of consumer legislation. It regulates to some extent the consumersupplier relations. Consumerists demand enforcement of discipline among the producers or manufacturers of food to ensure safety in the realm of food. Shri Rajmal Thakur S/O Late Shri Het Ram vs Food Safety Officer on 19 August, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45818632/ 3 The consumer's legitimate ignorance and his almost total dependence on the fairness and competence of those who supply his daily needs have made him a ready target for exploitation. The Act is intended to protect him against outright frauds. It does not provide for aggravation of offence based on the extent of contamination. Food pollution, even if it be only to the slightest extent, if continued in practice, would adversely affect the health of every man, woman and child in the country. Therefore the conclusion is that for an article of food when a standard has been fixed under the Act it has to be observed in every detail." 9. Hon'ble Supreme Court after taking into account all the judgments on this issue in Raj Kumar Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) 9 SCC 427, interalia held as under: "7.We are of the considered view that once standards are laid down by the legislature then those standards have to be followed. In items like milk which is a primary food, under the Act, it is not necessary to also prove that the food item had become unfit for human consumption or injurious to health. In this case, the only question to be determined is whether the article complies with the standards laid down or not? makes it mandatory that no person shall manufacture, distribute, sell or expose for sale or despatch or deliver to any agent or broker for the purpose of sale, any packaged food products which are not marked and labelled in the manner as may be specified by regulations. Section 26 (2)(ii) FSS Act also mandates that no food business operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacture, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter. It provides that the manufacturer or packer of an article of food shall be liable for such article of food if it does not meet the requirements of this Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder.
